In probabilistic terms, the aforementioned infinitely divisible process is equal to the conditional cumulative hazard process associated with the exchangeable sequence of random variables with minimum (or maximum) infinitely divisible marginals. Our results provide an analytic umbrella which embeds the de Finetti subfamilies of many interesting classes of multivariate distributions, such as exogenous shock models, exponential and geometric laws with lack-of-memory property, min-stable multivariate exponential and extreme-value distributions, as well as reciprocal Archimedean copulas with completely monotone generator and Archimedean copulas with log-completely monotone generator.

A new calibration method for H-fs-TALIF is proposed, and the ratio of two-photon absorption cross-sections, $ sigma^{(2)}$, for atomic hydrogen (H) and krypton (Kr) is determined for the broadband emission of a femtosecond laser system. The estimated ratio of the two-photon absorption cross-sections for H and Kr is $ sigma^{(2)}$ for H and Kr $ sigma^{(2)}$(Kr)/$ sigma^{(2)}$(H) = $0.027 pm 20$%, which is nearly twenty times lower than values previously obtained with narrowband nanosecond lasers. This discrepancy highlights the need for independent calibration of TALIF measurements for a specific laser pulsewidth range.

Recovering images from optical interferometric observations is one of the major challenges in the field. Unlike the case of observations at radio wavelengths, in the optical the atmospheric turbulence changes the phases on a very short time scale, which results in corrupted phase measurements. In order to overcome these limitations, several groups developed image reconstruction techniques based only on squared visibility and closure phase information, which are unaffected by atmospheric turbulence. We present the results of two techniques used by our group, which employed coherently integrated data from the Navy Prototype Optical Interferometer. Based on these techniques we were able to recover complex visibilities for several sources and image them using standard radio imaging software. We describe these techniques, the corrections applied to the data, present the images of a few sources, and discuss the implications of these results.

We embed spherical Rindler space -- a geometry with a spherical hole in its center -- in asymptotically AdS spacetime and show that it carries a gravitational entropy proportional to the area of the hole. Spherical AdS-Rindler space is holographically dual to an ultraviolet sector of the boundary field theory given by restriction to a strip of finite duration in time. Because measurements have finite durations, local observers in the field theory can only access information about bounded spatial regions. We propose a notion of Residual Entropy that captures uncertainty about the state of a system left by the collection of local, finite-time observables. For two-dimensional conformal field theories we use holography and the strong subadditivity of entanglement to propose a formula for Residual Entropy and show that it precisely reproduces the areas of circular holes in AdS3. Extending the notion to field theories on strips with variable durations in time, we show more generally that Residual Entropy computes the areas of all closed, inhomogenous curves on a spatial slice of AdS3. We discuss the extension to higher dimensional field theories, the relation of Residual Entropy to entanglement between scales, and some implications for the emergence of space from the RG flow of entangled field theories.

In this paper, we find a family $SL^{n,m}$, in any arbitrary dimensions, of cohomologically rigid solvable Lie superalgebras with nilradical the model filiform Lie superalgebra $L^{n,m}$. Moreover, we exhibit a family of cohomologically rigid solvable Lie superalgebras with nilradical the model nilpotent Lie superalgebra of generic characteristic sequence. Both cases correspond to solvable Lie superalgebras of maximal dimension for a given nilradical. Contrariwise, we will show that the family of Lie superalgebras $SL^{n,m}$ can be deformed if defined over a field of odd characteristic.

Existences of vector-like quarks (VLQs) are predicted in many new physics scenarios beyond the Standard Model (SM). We study the possibility of detecting the vector-like bottom quark (VLQ-$B$) being the $SU(2)$ singlet with electric charge $-1/3$ at the Large Hadron Electron Collider (LHeC) in a model-independent framework. The decay properties and single production of VLQ-$B$ at the LHeC are explored. Three types of signatures are investigated. By carrying out a fast simulation for the signals and the corresponding backgrounds, the signal significances are obtained. Our numerical results show that detecting of VLQ-$B$ via the semileptonic channel is better than via the fully hadronic or leptonic channel.

The pharmacopeia used by physicians and lay people in medieval Europe has largely been dismissed as placebo or superstition. While we now recognise that some of the materia medica used by medieval physicians could have had useful biological properties, research in this area is limited by the labour-intensive process of searching and interpreting historical medical texts. Here, we demonstrate the potential power of turning medieval medical texts into contextualised electronic databases amenable to exploration by algorithm. We use established methodologies from network science to reveal statistically significant patterns in ingredient selection and usage in a key text, the fifteenth-century Lylye of Medicynes, focusing on remedies to treat symptoms of microbial infection. We discuss the potential that these patterns reflect rational medical decisions. In providing a worked example of data-driven textual analysis, we demonstrate the potential of this approach to encourage interdisciplinary collaboration and to shine a new light on the ethnopharmacology of historical medical texts.

Attosecond streaking of atomic photoemission holds the promise to provide unprecedented information on the release time of the photoelectron. We show that attosecond streaking phase shifts indeed contain timing (or spectral phase) information associated with the Eisenbud-Wigner-Smith time delay matrix of quantum scattering. However, this is only accessible if the influence of the streaking infrared (IR) field on the emission process is properly accounted for. The IR probe field can strongly modify the observed streaking phase shift. We show that the part of the phase shift ( time shift ) due to the interaction between the outgoing electron and the combined Coulomb and IR laser fields can be described classically. By contrast, the strong initial-state dependence of the streaking phase shift is only revealed through the solution of the time-dependent Schr  odinger equation in its full dimensionality. We find a time delay between the hydrogenic 2s and 2p initial states in He+ exceeding 20as for a wide range of IR intensities and XUV energies.

The radial drift and diffusion of dust particles in protoplanetary disks affect both the opacity and temperature of such disks as well as the location and timing of planetesimal formation. In this paper, we present results of numerical simulations of particle-gas dynamics in protoplanetary disks that include dust grains with various size distributions. We consider three scenarios in terms of particle size ranges, one where the Stokes number $ tau_{ rm{s}} = 10^{-1} - 10^0$, one where $ tau_{ rm{s}} = 10^{-4} - 10^{-1}$ and finally one where $ tau_{ rm{s}} = 10^{-3} - 10^{0}$. Moreover, we consider both discrete and continuous distributions in particle size. In accordance with previous works we find in our multi-species simulations that different particle sizes interact via the gas and as a result their dynamics changes compared to the single-species case. The larger species trigger the streaming instability and create turbulence that drives the diffusion of the solid materials. We measure the radial equilibrium velocity of the system and find that the radial drift velocity of the large particles is reduced in the multi-species simulations and that the small particle species move on average outwards. We also vary the steepness of the size distribution, such that the exponent of the solid number density distribution, $ rm{d} it{N}/ rm{d} it{a}  propto  it{a^{-q}}$, is either $q = 3$ or $q = 4$. We measure the scale height of the particles and observe that small grains are stirred up well above the sedimented midplane layer where the large particles reside. Our measured diffusion and drift parameters can be used in coagulation models for planet formation as well as to understand relative mixing of the components of primitive meteorites (matrix, chondrules and CAIs) prior to inclusion in their parent bodies.

We report the identification of LP 400-22 (WD 2234+222) as a very low-mass and high-velocity white dwarf. The ultraviolet GALEX and optical photometric colors and a spectral line analysis of LP 400-22 show this star to have an effective temperature of 11080+/-140 K and a surface gravity of log g = 6.32+/-0.08. Therefore, this is a helium core white dwarf with a mass of 0.17 M_solar. The tangential velocity of this white dwarf is 414+/-43 km/s, making it one of the fastest moving white dwarfs known. We discuss probable evolutionary scenarios for this remarkable object.

As in our previous work [1] we address the problem to determine the splitting of the normal bundle of rational curves. With apolarity theory we are able to characterize some particular subvarieties in some Hilbert scheme of rational curves, defined by the splitting type of the normal bundle and the restricted tangent bundle.

We describe two ground based observing campaigns aimed at building a grid of approximately 200 spectrophotometric standard stars (SPSS), with an internal ~1% precision and tied to Vega within ~3%, for the absolute flux calibration of data gathered by Gaia, the ESA astrometric mission. The criteria for the selection and a list of candidates are presented, together with a description of the survey strategy and the adopted data analysis methods. We also discuss a short list of notable rejected SPSS candidates and difficult cases, based on identification problems, literature discordant data, visual companions, and variability. In fact, all candidates are also monitored for constancy (within  pm5 mmag, approximately). In particular, we report on a CALSPEC standard, 1740346, that we found to be a delta Scuti variable during our short-term monitoring (1-2 h) campaign.

Fueled by both advances in robust optimization theory and applications of reinforcement learning, robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) have gained increasing attention, due to their powerful capability for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. This review provides an in-depth overview of the evolution and advances in RMDPs formulations, particularly in ambiguity modeling, and classifies these methods for representing uncertainty into three principal approaches: parametric, moment-based, and discrepancy-based, elaborating the trade-offs among the alternative representations. Meanwhile, the review delves into the rectangular assumptions, which guarantee the tractability of RMDPs yet are noted for their conservatism. The review summarizes three popular rectangular conditions and develops a new proof to attest to the NP-hardness of non-rectangular RMDPs. Out of the traditional RMDPs scope, recent efforts without conventional rectangular assumptions and new fashions within the RMDPs community are also reviewed. These studies foster the development of more flexible and practical modeling frameworks and enhance the adaptability and performance of RMDPs.

At high-energies the gluon-gluon fusion is the dominant mechanism of $c  bar c$ production. This process was calculated in the NLO collinear as well as in the k$_t$-factorization approaches in the past. We show that the present knowledge of gluon distributions does not allow to make a precise predictions for $c  bar c$ production at LHC, in particular at forward rapidities. In this paper we study production of $c  bar c$ pairs including several subleading mechanisms. This includes: $gg  to Q  bar Q$, $ gamma g  to Q  bar Q$, $g  gamma  to Q  bar Q$, $ gamma  gamma  to Q  bar Q$. In this context we use MRST-QED parton distributions which include photon as a parton in the proton as well as elastic photon distributions calculated in the equivalent photon approximation. We present distributions in the $c$ quark ($ bar c$ antiquark) rapidity and transverse momenta and compare them to the dominant gluon-gluon fusion contribution. We discuss also inclusive single and central diffractive processes using diffractive parton distribution found from the analysis of HERA diffractive data. As in the previous case we present distribution in $c$ ($ bar c$) rapidity and transverse momentum. Finally we present results for exclusive central diffractive mechanism discussed recently in the literature. We show corresponding differential distributions and compare them with corresponding distributions for single and central diffractive components.

Quantum steering, an intermediate quantum correlation lying between entanglement and nonlocality, has emerged as a critical quantum resource for a variety of quantum information processing tasks such as quantum key distribution and true randomness generation. The ability to detect and quantify quantum steering is crucial for these applications. Semi-definite programming (SDP) has proven to be a valuable tool to quantify quantum steering. However, the challenge lies in the fact that the optimal measurement strategy is not priori known, making it time-consuming to compute the steerable measure for any given quantum state. Furthermore, the utilization of SDP requires full information of the quantum state, necessitating quantum state tomography, which can be complex and resource-consuming. In this work, we utilize the semi-supervised self-training model to estimate the steerable weight, a pivotal measure of quantum steering. The model can be trained using a limited amount of labeled data, thus reducing the time for labeling. The features are constructed by the probabilities derived by performing three sets of projective measurements under arbitrary local unitary transformations on the target states, circumventing the need for quantum tomography. The model demonstrates robust generalization capabilities and can achieve high levels of precision with limited resources.

A description is provided of the software algorithms developed for the CMS tracker both for reconstructing charged-particle trajectories in proton-proton interactions and for using the resulting tracks to estimate the positions of the LHC luminous region and individual primary-interaction vertices. Despite the very hostile environment at the LHC, the performance obtained with these algorithms is found to be excellent. For ttbar events under typical 2011 pileup conditions, the average track-reconstruction efficiency for promptly-produced charged particles with transverse momenta of pt > 0.9 GeV is 94% for pseudorapidities of abs(eta) < 0.9 and 85% for 0.9 < abs(eta) < 2.5. The inefficiency is caused mainly by hadrons that undergo nuclear interactions in the tracker material. For isolated muons, the corresponding efficiencies are essentially 100%. For isolated muons of pt = 100 GeV emitted at abs(eta) < 1.4, the resolutions are approximately 2.8% in pt, and respectively, 10 microns and 30 microns in the transverse and longitudinal impact parameters. The position resolution achieved for reconstructed primary vertices that correspond to interesting pp collisions is 10-12 microns in each of the three spatial dimensions. The tracking and vertexing software is fast and flexible, and easily adaptable to other functions, such as fast tracking for the trigger, or dedicated tracking for electrons that takes into account bremsstrahlung.

In smooth and convex multiobjective optimization problems the set of Pareto optima is diffeomorphic to an $m-1$ dimensional simplex, where $m$ is the number of objective functions. The vertices of the simplex are the optima of the individual functions and the $(k-1)$-dimensional facets are the Pareto optimal set of $k$ functions subproblems. Such a hierarchy of submanifolds is a geometrical object called stratification and the union of such manifolds, in this case the set of Pareto optima, is called a stratified set. We discuss how these geometrical structures generalize in the non convex cases, we survey the known results and deduce possible suggestions for the design of dedicated optimization strategies.

In recent years, large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have been pivotal in advancing various artificial intelligence applications, including natural language processing and software engineering. A promising yet underexplored area is utilizing LLMs in software testing, particularly in black-box testing. This paper explores the test cases devised by ChatGPT in comparison to those created by human participants. In this study, ChatGPT (GPT-4) and four participants each created black-box test cases for three applications based on specifications written by the authors. The goal was to evaluate the real-world applicability of the proposed test cases, identify potential shortcomings, and comprehend how ChatGPT could enhance human testing strategies. ChatGPT can generate test cases that generally match or slightly surpass those created by human participants in terms of test viewpoint coverage. Additionally, our experiments demonstrated that when ChatGPT cooperates with humans, it can cover considerably more test viewpoints than each can achieve alone, suggesting that collaboration between humans and ChatGPT may be more effective than human pairs working together. Nevertheless, we noticed that the test cases generated by ChatGPT have certain issues that require addressing before use.

In a previous work of the first authors, a non-holonomic model, generalising the micromorphic models and allowing for curvature (disclinations) to arise from the kinematic values, was presented. In the present paper, a generalisation of the classical models of Euler-Bernoulli and Timoshenko bending beams based on the mentioned work is proposed. The former is still composed of only one unidimensional scalar field, while the later introduces a third unidimensional scalar field, correcting the second order terms. The generalised Euler-Bernoulli beam is then shown to exhibit curvature (i.e. disclinations) linked to a third order derivative of the displacement, but no torsion (dislocations). Parallelly, the generalised Timoshenko beam is shown to exhibit both curvature and torsion, where the former is linked to the non-holonomy introduced in the generalisation. Lastly, using variational calculus, asymptotic values for the value taken by the curvature in static equilibrium are obtained when the second order contribution becomes negligible; along with an equation for the torsion in the generalised Timoshenko beam.

We consider a Sklyanin algebra S with 3 generators, which is the quadratic algebra over a field k with three generators x,y,z given by three relations pxy+qyx+rzz=0, pyz+qzy+rxx=0 and pzx+qxz+ryy=0, where p,q,r are parameters from the fileld k. This class of algebras enjoyed much of attention, in particular, using tools from algebraic geometry, Feigin & Odesskii, and Artin, Tate & Van den Berg, showed that if at least two of the parameters p, q and r are non-zero and at least two of three numbers p^3,q^3 and r^3 are distinct, then S is Koszul and has the same Hilbert series as the algebra of commutative polynomials in three variables. It became commonly accepted, that it is impossible to achieve the same objective by purely algebraic and combinatorial means, like the Groebner basis technique. The main purpose of this paper is to trace combinatorial meaning of the properties of Sklyanin algebras, such as Koszulity, PBW, PHS, Calabi-Yau, and to give a new constructive proof of the above facts due to Artin, Tate and Van den Bergh.   Further, we study a wider class of Sklyanin algebras, namely the situation when all parameters of relations could be different. This class called generalized Sklyanin algebras. We classify up to isomorphism genralized Sklyanin algebras with polynomial Hilbert series. We show that generalized Slyanin algebras in general position have the Golod-Shafarevich Hilbert series (with exception of the case of the field with two elements).

In this paper, we review observational aspects of three common small-scale energetic events in the solar transition region (TR), namely: TR explosive events, ultraviolet bursts and jets. These events are defined in either (both) spectral or (and) imaging data. The development of multiple instruments capable of observing the TR has allowed researchers to gain numerous insights into these phenomena in recent years. These events have provided a proxy to study how mass and energy are transported between the solar chromosphere and the corona. As the physical mechanisms responsible for these small-scale events might be similar to the mechanisms responsible for large-scale phenomena, such as flares and coronal mass ejections, analysis of these events could also help our understanding of the solar atmosphere from small to large scales. The observations of these small-scale energetic events demonstrate that the TR is extremely dynamic and is a crucial layer in the solar atmosphere between the chromosphere and the corona.

Wearable egocentric cameras and machine learning have the potential to provide clinicians with a more nuanced understanding of patient hand use at home after stroke and spinal cord injury (SCI). However, they require detailed contextual information (i.e., activities and object interactions) to effectively interpret metrics and meaningfully guide therapy planning. We demonstrate that an object-centric approach, focusing on what objects patients interact with rather than how they move, can effectively recognize Activities of Daily Living (ADL) in real-world rehabilitation settings. We evaluated our models on a complex dataset collected in the wild comprising 2261 minutes of egocentric video from 16 participants with impaired hand function. By leveraging pre-trained object detection and hand-object interaction models, our system achieves robust performance across different impairment levels and environments, with our best model achieving a mean weighted F1-score of 0.78 +/- 0.12 and maintaining an F1-score > 0.5 for all participants using leave-one-subject-out cross validation. Through qualitative analysis, we observe that this approach generates clinically interpretable information about functional object use while being robust to patient-specific movement variations, making it particularly suitable for rehabilitation contexts with prevalent upper limb impairment.

We analytically prove that the existence of the delta-function singularity in the chirally-odd twist-3 distribution $e(x)$ of the nucleon is inseparably connected with the nonvanishing quark condensate as a signal of the spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking of the QCD vacuum. This singularity in $e(x)$, which would be observed as a sizable violation of the 1st moment sum rule, is then interpreted as giving a very rare case that the nontrivial vacuum structure of QCD manifests in an observable of a localized QCD excitation, i.e. the nucleon.

Functional data analysis has been extensively conducted. In this study, we consider a partially functional model, under which some covariates are scalars and have linear effects, while some other variables are functional and have unspecified nonlinear effects. Significantly advancing from the existing literature, we consider a model with interactions between the functional and scalar covariates. To accommodate long-tailed error distributions which are not uncommon in data analysis, we adopt the quantile technique for estimation. To achieve more interpretable estimation, and to accommodate many practical settings, we assume that the functional covariate effects are locally sparse (that is, there exist subregions on which the effects are exactly zero), which naturally leads to a variable/model selection problem. We propose respecting the  main effect, interaction  hierarchy, which postulates that if a subregion has a nonzero effect in an interaction term, then its effect has to be nonzero in the corresponding main functional effect. For estimation, identification of local sparsity, and respect of the hierarchy, we propose a penalization approach. An effective computational algorithm is developed, and the consistency properties are rigorously established under mild regularity conditions. Simulation shows the practical effectiveness of the proposed approach. The analysis of the Tecator data further demonstrates its practical applicability. Overall, this study can deliver a novel and practically useful model and a statistically and numerically satisfactory estimation approach.

A commonly used technique for managing AI complexity in real-time strategy (RTS) games is to use action and/or state abstractions. High-level abstractions can often lead to good strategic decision making, but tactical decision quality may suffer due to lost details. A competing method is to sample the search space which often leads to good tactical performance in simple scenarios, but poor high-level planning.   We propose to use a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to select among a limited set of abstract action choices, and to utilize the remaining computation time for game tree search to improve low level tactics. The CNN is trained by supervised learning on game states labelled by Puppet Search, a strategic search algorithm that uses action abstractions. The network is then used to select a script --- an abstract action --- to produce low level actions for all units. Subsequently, the game tree search algorithm improves the tactical actions of a subset of units using a limited view of the game state only considering units close to opponent units.   Experiments in the microRTS game show that the combined algorithm results in higher win-rates than either of its two independent components and other state-of-the-art microRTS agents.   To the best of our knowledge, this is the first successful application of a convolutional network to play a full RTS game on standard game maps, as previous work has focused on sub-problems, such as combat, or on very small maps.

Tool learning has emerged as a promising direction by extending Large Language Models' (LLMs) capabilities with external tools. Existing tool learning studies primarily focus on the general-purpose tool-use capability, which addresses explicit user requirements in instructions. However, they overlook the importance of personalized tool-use capability, leading to an inability to handle implicit user preferences. To address the limitation, we first formulate the task of personalized tool learning, which integrates user's interaction history towards personalized tool usage. To fill the gap of missing benchmarks, we construct PEToolBench, featuring diverse user preferences reflected in interaction history under three distinct personalized settings, and encompassing a wide range of tool-use scenarios. Moreover, we propose a framework PEToolLLaMA to adapt LLMs to the personalized tool learning task, which is trained through supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization. Extensive experiments on PEToolBench demonstrate the superiority of PEToolLLaMA over existing LLMs.

Renewable energy sources and further electrificationof energy consumption are key enablers for decreasing green-house gas emissions, but also introduce increased complexitywithin the electric power system. The increased availability ofautomation, information and communication technology, andintelligent solutions for system operation have transformed thepower system into a smart grid. In order to support thedevelopment process of smart grid solutions on the system level,testing has to be done in a holistic manner, covering the multi-domain aspect of such complex systems. This paper introducesthe concept of holistic power system testing and discuss first stepstowards a corresponding methodology that is being developed inthe European ERIGrid research infrastructure project.

We propose a new procedure for parton-to-hadron fragmentation in proton-proton collisions. The hadronization is considered in the parton-parton center-of-mass system and hadrons are assumed to be emitted in the direction of outgoing partons in that frame and then their four-momenta are transformed to the overall center-of-mass system using relevant Lorentz transformations and appropriate distributions are constructed. For heavy hadron production the energy-momentum condition is imposed. In many cases our procedure disagrees with the commonly used rule that rapidity of produced hadron is the same as rapidity of the parent parton. We illustrate the newly proposed scheme for production of $D$ mesons, $ Lambda_c$ baryon and $ eta_c$ quarkonium in leading-order approach to parton production. The transverse momentum, rapidity and Feynman-$x_F$ distributions are shown. We consider $c  to D$ and $g  to D$ as well as $c  to  eta_c$ and $g  to  eta_c$ hadronization processes. The resulting rapidity distributions are much narrower than those obtained in the traditional approach with parton-hadron rapidity equivalence. This has consequences both for mid- and forward rapidities and could have consequences for high-energy neutrino production in the Earth's atmosphere. We discuss also $c  to  Lambda_c^+$ and $b  to  Lambda_c^+$ fragmentation and find that the second mechanism could be partly responsible for the enhanced production of $ Lambda_c^{ pm}$ observed recently by the ALICE collaboration.

Robust and generalized tool manipulation requires an understanding of the properties and affordances of different tools. We investigate whether linguistic information about a tool (e.g., its geometry, common uses) can help control policies adapt faster to new tools for a given task. We obtain diverse descriptions of various tools in natural language and use pre-trained language models to generate their feature representations. We then perform language-conditioned meta-learning to learn policies that can efficiently adapt to new tools given their corresponding text descriptions. Our results demonstrate that combining linguistic information and meta-learning significantly accelerates tool learning in several manipulation tasks including pushing, lifting, sweeping, and hammering.

The dynamics of two-level systems in time-dependent backgrounds is under consideration. We present some new exact solutions in special backgrounds decaying in time. On the other hand, following ideas of Feynman, Vernon and Hellwarth, we discuss in detail the possibility to reduce the quantum dynamics to a classical Hamiltonian system. This, in particular, opens the possibility to directly apply powerful methods of classical mechanics (e.g. KAM methods) to study the quantum system. Following such an approach, we draw conclusions of relevance for ``quantum chaos'' when the external background is periodic or quasi-periodic in time.

We find an exact solution of the equations of motion of a two-field cosmological model, which realizes multi-field dark energy. This study investigates the two-dimensional ferromagnetic Ising model incorporating long-range interactions.  Monte Carlo simulations reveal that, within an intermediate range of interaction strengths, long-range interactions exert a dominant influence compared to short-range interactions.  A subsequent renormalization group analysis suggests a method for quantifying the impact of long-range interactions by treating them as an effective dimensional change.

This paper addresses the challenge of novel-view rendering human performers wearing clothing with complex textures from a sparse set of camera views. While recent works have demonstrated impressive rendering quality for humans with relatively uniform textures using sparse views, performance degrades significantly with intricate patterns due to limitations in recovering the high-frequency geometric details present in the input views.  To overcome this limitation, we introduce HDhuman, a novel framework for human reconstruction and rendering.  This framework comprises a human reconstruction network, incorporating a pixel-aligned spatial transformer, and a rendering network, leveraging geometry-guided pixel-wise feature integration.

The pixel-aligned spatial transformer in the reconstruction network computes correlations across input views to enhance the recovered high-frequency details in the reconstructed human shape.  This refined surface reconstruction, in turn, guides the geometry-guided pixel-wise visibility reasoning within the rendering network.  This process facilitates multi-view feature integration, enabling the rendering network to produce high-quality 2K resolution images of novel views.  Crucially, unlike previous neural rendering approaches, which often require training or fine-tuning separate networks for each scene, HDhuman is a generalizable framework, capable of adapting to novel subjects.

This study investigates the phase diagram of the Abelian-Higgs model in one spatial and one temporal dimension (1+1D) on a lattice.  A line of first-order phase transitions is observed, demarcating the Higgs phase from the confined phase.  This transition line terminates at a quantum critical point (QCP).  Above this QCP, the two phases are connected by a smooth crossover.  Analysis of the QCP reveals compelling evidence supporting a description as a product of two non-interacting systems: a massless free fermion and a massless free boson.  However, certain unexpected results emerge, challenging the validity of this simplified picture and suggesting the novel nature of this critical point.

This paper examines the phenomenology of neutrino oscillations arising from solar, atmospheric, supernova, and laboratory sources. A critical review of analytical expressions describing matter effects on neutrino propagation is presented.

The formation of neutron stars (NSs), resulting from both the collapse of massive stars and the merger of compact objects, is often characterized by luminous transient phenomena emanating from explosively ejected material.  Specifically, if the nascent NSs possess millisecond rotation periods and sufficiently strong magnetic fields, the spin-down process can release substantial energy into the surrounding ejecta.  This energy release can lead to the production of superluminous supernovae in cases of massive stellar collapse.  In contrast, NS mergers and accretion-induced collapses of white dwarfs might generate unusual, rapidly evolving, and luminous optical transients.  Critically, if the dipolar magnetic fields of the newly formed NSs are amplified to values as high as 10<sup>15</sup> G, a relativistic jet can be launched.  Subsequent breakout of this jet from the surrounding, nearly isotropic ejecta can produce a gamma-ray burst.

This study investigates finite-temperature phase transitions in Bose-Fermi-Hubbard systems employing the self-consistent random phase approximation (RPA).  Focusing on the hard-core boson limit and utilizing pseudospin formalism, we calculate the density-density correlator within the RPA framework.  The analysis explores the potential for transitions from the superfluid to supersolid phases.  Our results demonstrate that transitions between uniform and charge-ordered phases exhibit either second-order or first-order character, contingent upon the specific system parameters.

This study establishes a rigorous connection between quantum circuit complexity and approximate quantum error correction (AQEC) capabilities, crucial properties for the physics and practical application of quantum many-body systems.  The analysis encompasses both all-to-all connected systems and geometric scenarios, including lattice systems in finite spatial dimensions.  To quantify AQEC performance, a new code parameter, subsystem variance, is introduced.  This parameter exhibits a strong correlation with the optimal AQEC precision.

A key finding is that for a code encoding \(k\) logical qubits within \(n\) physical qubits, if the subsystem variance falls below an \(O(k/n)\) threshold, then any state within the code subspace must satisfy certain lower bounds on circuit complexity.  These lower bounds characterize non-trivial phases of the code.  Based on these results, an \(O(k/n)\) threshold is proposed to distinguish code subspaces that exhibit AQEC from those that do not.

This theory of AQEC provides a comprehensive framework for understanding quantum complexity and order in many-body quantum systems.  It offers new insights into various physical scenarios, particularly topological order and critical quantum systems, areas of significant importance in many-body and high-energy physics.

The circular restricted three-body problem, modeling a body of negligible mass orbiting a star and a planet in a circular orbit, predicts five Lagrangian points as equilibrium points. However, the derivation of these points assumes the sole influence of gravitational forces. This assumption is not valid for dust particles, which are subject to additional forces, including radiation pressure. We therefore investigate the equilibrium points for dust particles in the circular restricted three-body problem augmented by radiation forces. Our analysis reveals that the equilibrium points for dust particles lie on curves connecting the Lagrangian points of the gravitational-only problem. The distribution of these radiation-influenced equilibrium points differs significantly depending on the central star-planet system's characteristics. For example, the substantial mass of Jupiter results in a broad range of heliocentric distances for its equilibrium points. Vector meson global spin alignment provides a potent diagnostic for characterizing the vorticity field in non-central relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This study introduces a methodology for mitigating the influence of limited pseudo-rapidity coverage in extracting the azimuthal dependence of the spin alignment parameter, ρ<sub>00</sub>.  The proposed method explicitly accounts for the impact of finite pseudo-rapidity acceptance on the azimuthal anisotropy of φ meson spin alignment, while also considering the potential contribution of intrinsic spin alignment.  Validation of the method is achieved through Monte Carlo simulations, confirming its efficacy in enabling precise and accurate determination of the azimuthal dependence of global spin alignment.

This study introduces novel subclasses of Petri nets, termed "receptor Petri nets" and "effector Petri nets."  The integration or removal of these substructures within the primary Petri net architecture is governed by the principles of fusion and defusion.  Specifically, two pairs of entities—position-marking receptors/effectors and transition-marking receptors/effectors—are posited.  These entities facilitate the monitoring of key parameters within the primary net and, when appropriate, enable their dynamic regulation.

This paper investigates the multi-marginal partial optimal transport (POT) problem for $m$ discrete, unbalanced measures, each with a support of at most $n$ points.  We establish two equivalent formulations of this multi-marginal POT problem in terms of the multi-marginal optimal transport problem.  Crucially, we extend the cost tensor to achieve these equivalences.

The first equivalent formulation holds under the constraint that the total masses of the measures are sufficiently close.  The second formulation, however, relaxes this constraint, but necessitates a more intricate extended cost tensor structure.  Our proof techniques leverage novel graph-theoretic mass-shifting procedures to guide the transportation plan towards optimal regions.

Based on these equivalent formulations, we introduce an optimization algorithm, termed ApproxMPOT, which builds upon the Sinkhorn algorithm for solving the entropically regularized multi-marginal optimal transport problem.  Computational analysis reveals that the ApproxMPOT algorithm approximates the optimal value of the multi-marginal POT problem with a time complexity upper bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(m^3(n+1)^m / \varepsilon^2)$, where $\varepsilon > 0$ represents the desired tolerance.

This study introduces a novel algorithm for determining the equilibrium configurations of fluctuating, continuous elastic filaments.  Employing a hybrid approach rooted in statistical mechanics and differential geometry, the algorithm facilitates the calculation of the probability distribution function for the end-to-end distance of filaments exhibiting non-zero spontaneous curvature.  Analysis reveals a critical temperature regime where filaments with low twist and high bending rigidity exhibit near-complete stretching.  Furthermore, the algorithm's capacity to incorporate volume interactions is demonstrated through the calculation of excluded volume effects on the filament's end-to-end distance.

This paper presents a novel representation of three-dimensional rotations, leveraging the inherent projective space structure.  This fundamental geometric property, hitherto unexploited in computer science, is exploited to parameterize rotations using four affine patches.  This approach offers significant advantages over existing methods.  Specifically, the affine patch representation is more compact than quaternions (requiring only ratios of linear or quadratic polynomials for computations), encompassing the entire rotation group without singularities, a critical distinction from Euler angles and rotation vectors.  Unlike Euler angle and rotation vector representations, which necessitate transcendental functions for basic operations, the affine patch formalism relies solely on polynomial expressions.  Illustrative of the method's utility, the paper derives the differential equation for integrating angular velocity using this affine patch formalism.  This equation exhibits the same computational complexity as its quaternion counterpart while avoiding the quaternion's requirement for normalization and associated issues with non-zero vectors in the state space.

This study investigates the performance of sorting algorithms within a dynamic data environment, characterized by evolving input data during execution.  Instead of a static final output, algorithms in this framework strive to maintain an output closely approximating the correct ordering for the data's current state, iteratively refining their estimated solution.  We demonstrate that a straightforward repeated insertion-sort algorithm achieves a high-probability bound of O(n) Kendall τ distance between the maintained list and the underlying total order of n elements.  This result is established within a dynamic model wherein each comparison is immediately followed by a random swap of two adjacent elements within the underlying total order.  Crucially, this result achieves asymptotic optimality, aligning with the Ω(n) lower bound established for Kendall τ distance in this problem context.  This finding effectively bridges the gap between the established lower bound and the previously best-performing algorithm, which exhibited a high-probability O(n log log n) Kendall τ distance.  Further, this outcome corroborates previous empirical findings that suggest insertion sort's practical superiority over quicksort in scenarios involving dynamic data.

This paper introduces CrowdX, a novel, large-scale, accurately-labeled crowd counting dataset featuring parameterized realizations and high fidelity.  We demonstrate that leveraging CrowdX for data augmentation significantly enhances the performance of the efficient benchmark network, ESA-Net, by 8.4%.  Similar performance gains are observed for the pre-trained MCNN and CSRNet architectures, further validating the dataset's utility.

While various factors, including background complexity, camera angle, crowd density, and image resolution, influence crowd counting accuracy, existing research lacks a comprehensive understanding of their specific impact.  CrowdX's rich annotation allows for a data-driven analysis of these critical parameters.  Extensive comparative experiments using this dataset provide valuable insights into the nuanced relationships between these factors and crowd counting performance, offering practical guidance for algorithm deployment.  This research provides a crucial foundation for a deeper understanding of the challenges in crowd counting and suggests actionable recommendations for practitioners.

Despite extensive investigation of exciton relaxation within transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), the spatial propagation of excitons has remained comparatively understudied, despite its pivotal role in optoelectronic applications and the manifestation of intriguing unconventional behaviours, such as spatial halos.  This work scrutinizes the spatiotemporal dynamics of excitons in TMDs, meticulously tracking their evolution in time, momentum, and spatial coordinates.  Specifically, we examine the temperature-dependent exciton diffusion, encompassing the intricate exciton landscape defined by the interplay of bright and dark states. Employing a fully quantum mechanical formalism, we demonstrate an unexpected negative transient diffusion at low temperatures. This counterintuitive phenomenon arises from the presence of dark exciton states within TMDs, stemming from the intricate interplay between spatial exciton diffusion and intervalley exciton-phonon scattering.

While layered transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), exemplified by MX<sub>2</sub> (M = Mo, W; X = S, Se, Te), have garnered considerable attention for their topological properties, the fundamental mechanism underlying their topological phase transitions (TPTs) remains obscure.  Conventional paradigms posit that non-trivial band topology in TMDs arises from band inversion between metal d and chalcogen p orbitals, with the former experiencing a downward shift relative to the latter.  However, our analysis reveals a divergent scenario in TMDs, demonstrably distinct from the established theoretical framework.  Specifically, MS<sub>2</sub> and MSe<sub>2</sub> exhibit an inverse TPT, characterized by the chalcogen p orbitals descending below the metal d orbitals.  Intriguingly, in MTe<sub>2</sub>, the TPT occurs through inversion between metal d orbitals.  These findings challenge the prevailing conceptualization of TPTs and provide critical insights for elucidating the topological characteristics of emergent topological materials.

Decision-making within identical contexts often exhibits heterogeneity stemming from individual predilections and experiential backgrounds.  This variability is demonstrably evident in disparate judicial responses to drug-related offenses or differing treatment protocols employed by medical professionals.  Consequently, identifying contextual factors engendering substantial inter-decision-maker disagreement is a critical endeavor.  This study formulates this challenge as a causal inference problem, specifically targeting regions where the selection of the decision-maker exerts a substantial causal influence on the final decision.  A novel algorithm is proposed, which optimizes an empirical objective function to pinpoint these regions of heterogeneity.  A theoretical generalization bound is provided to quantify the algorithm's performance guarantees.  Empirical validation using a semi-synthetic dataset demonstrates that the algorithm accurately recovers the target regions of heterogeneity, surpassing baseline methods.  Finally, the algorithm's efficacy is further corroborated by its application to real-world healthcare datasets, where it identifies patterns of variability concordant with established clinical understanding.

Precise determinations of global parton distribution functions (PDFs) necessitate the incorporation of theoretical uncertainties, especially as data quality improves.  This study presents NNPDF4.0, a next-generation global proton PDF set, incorporating theoretical uncertainties arising from the inclusion of heavy nuclear and deuteron data in the fitting procedure.  These uncertainties are estimated by comparing nuclear observable predictions derived from nuclear PDFs with those from proton PDFs.  For heavy nuclear targets, the nNNPDF2.0 set is employed.  For deuteron data, an iterative procedure is developed to simultaneously determine proton and deuteron PDFs, with each set incorporating uncertainties propagated from the other.  The inclusion of nuclear uncertainties helps reconcile discrepancies observed in the global proton PDF fit, particularly those between nuclear data and the extended LHC dataset utilized in NNPDF4.0.

This paper investigates gradient estimation for a network of nonlinear stochastic units, the Little model.  Many machine learning architectures are structured as networks of homogeneous units, and the Little model's generality encompasses several prominent architectures.  However, the absence of a closed-form solution for the stationary distribution precludes the application of gradient methods prevalent in similar models, such as Boltzmann machines or sigmoid belief networks.  To circumvent this limitation, a novel approach to derivative calculation is introduced, leveraging measure-valued differentiation and simultaneous perturbation.  This method extends prior work on gradient estimation algorithms, which were often confined to networks exhibiting restrictive properties, such as symmetry or acyclic connectivity.

This study investigates sequence similarity detection via gap-penalty alignment, leveraging a recently developed theoretical framework rooted in the morphology of alignment paths.  Analysis reveals that alignments of uncorrelated sequences exhibit scale-invariant statistical properties.  This invariance forms the cornerstone of a scaling theory for alignments of correlated sequences.  Employing a simplified Markov model of evolutionary processes, we generate sequences with precisely defined interdependencies and establish a rigorous, unambiguous metric for alignment fidelity.  The resulting scaling theory predicts a direct relationship between alignment fidelity, alignment parameters, and the statistical parameters governing sequence correlations.  The theory further yields explicit criteria for optimizing alignment parameters.  These theoretical predictions are validated through extensive numerical simulations.

Previous sections contextualize Yang-Mills theory historically and detail relevant aspects of the field strength.  The concluding section demonstrates how Yang-Mills theory, combined with spontaneous symmetry breaking, the Goldstone theorem, and subsequent developments, contributed to the Standard Model of particle physics.

This study addresses this limitation by leveraging probabilistic machine learning techniques to delineate and quantify higher-order features embedded within methylation profiles. Crucially, these features transcend the limitations of simple averages by capturing the intricate spatial correlations inherent in methylation patterns across genomic regions. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the clustering of promoter-proximal regions based on distinct methylation profiles. Analysis reveals five major methylation patterns across diverse cell lines, providing compelling evidence that methylation patterns extending beyond CpG islands contribute to gene expression regulation. A rigorous analysis of both the standard and an approximate Newton-Raphson algorithm is undertaken, considering both master-slave and island operational modes under droop control strategies. The theoretical framework is substantiated through comprehensive computational simulations.

This paper addresses the critical issue of parcel loss prediction within the e-commerce last-mile delivery paradigm. The proliferation of data encompassing product, customer, and order details has facilitated the application of machine learning to this problem. However, the inherent class imbalance, with a negligible proportion of parcels experiencing loss, presents a significant methodological challenge. To overcome this, we introduce two novel machine learning approaches: Data Balance with Supervised Learning (DBSL) and Deep Hybrid Ensemble Learning (DHEL). These models aim to enhance accuracy in predicting parcel loss, thereby providing valuable insights for e-commerce retailers to optimize insurance strategies and mitigate financial risks. Recent advancements in transmission electron microscopy (TEM) have facilitated more precise visualization of materials and physical processes, such as metal oxidation.  However, the quality of this visualization is often compromised by electron beam-induced damage, specimen movement, and environmental fluctuations.  To mitigate these limitations, a novel image registration method has been developed. This method involves acquiring a sequence of low-dose TEM images and computationally registering them.  This registration process, analogous to a prefix sum operation, necessitates a computationally intensive binary operator.  The processing of extended image series necessitates parallelization.  Our parallelization scheme, implemented on 512 Intel Ivy Bridge cores, significantly accelerates the registration process.  The time required to process images acquired over a ten-second period has been reduced from approximately thirteen hours to less than seven minutes.

This paper investigates the determinants of irreducible representations within the generalized symmetric groups, specifically $\mathbb{Z}_r \wr S_n$.  A precise formula is derived for computing the determinant of any irreducible representation of this group.  Existing literature has addressed the characterization and enumeration of irreducible representations possessing non-trivial determinants within finite groups.  Building upon these precedents, for a given positive integer $n$, an odd prime $r$, and a non-trivial multiplicative character $\zeta$ of $\mathbb{Z}_r \wr S_n$ where $n < r$, we present a closed-form expression for $N_\zeta(n)$, the count of irreducible representations of $\mathbb{Z}_r \wr S_n$ whose determinant aligns with $\zeta$.

This study investigates exact solutions to the vacuum Einstein field equations with a cosmological constant in spacetime admitting a three-parameter isometry group with two-dimensional spacelike orbits.  These solutions, expressed in advanced and retarded null coordinates, incorporate two arbitrary functions, a consequence of the freedom in choosing null coordinates.  Applying the Israel junction conditions in the thin-wall approximation yields a single constraint equation governing these two functions within spherical, planar, and hyperbolic domain wall spacetimes exhibiting reflection symmetry.  The remaining coordinate freedom is uniquely determined by the requirement that the metric solutions reduce to known solutions when the domain wall surface energy density, σ₀, vanishes.  This requirement leads to a conformally flat planar domain wall solution within a de Sitter universe.

This paper investigates the first-order theory of the structure $(\mathbb{Q}_p, G)$, where $G$ is a multiplicative subgroup of the $p$-adic rationals $\mathbb{Q}_p$ satisfying the Mann property and being a small subset within a first-order structure.

This includes an axiomatization of the group $G$ as a valued group, where the valuation is induced by the $p$-adic valuation on $\mathbb{Q}_p$.  Crucially, we consider the case where the subgroups $G^{[n]}$ of $G$ have finite index for all $n$.

Under this condition, we characterize the definable sets within this theory and demonstrate that the theory is NIP (not the independence property).

This study investigates the carrier concentration bistabilities emerging in a highly photo-excited electron gas.  The kinetics of this non-equilibrium electron system are governed by a set of nonlinear rate equations.  At low temperatures and continuous-wave photoexcitation, these equations exhibit three steady-state solutions within a specific photo-excitation energy range, contingent upon electron-electron interaction strength.  Two of these solutions are stable, while the third is unstable.  Furthermore, the hysteresis loop characterizing these bistabilities is derived.  A diffusion model is developed, enabling the coexistence of two spatially separated homogeneous phases within the non-equilibrium electron gas.  The order parameter, defined as the difference in electron population at the conduction band minimum between the two stable steady states, is determined by a Maxwell construction derived from a generalized free energy functional.  This order parameter vanishes as the system approaches the critical curve, signifying a non-equilibrium first-order phase transition.

Assessing the complexity of classification problems is a crucial aspect of supervised machine learning, underpinning meta-learning approaches. This novel tool significantly expands the accessibility of these analyses within the machine learning community, facilitating research in the most prevalent programming environment.

Human pose estimation (HPE) is crucial for developing context-aware AI systems within operating rooms (ORs). This demonstrates the feasibility of deploying accurate HPE systems in OR environments while mitigating privacy risks.

Multi-armed bandit (MAB) and stochastic linear bandit (SLB) problems are central to reinforcement learning.  Classical algorithms for these problems with a time horizon of $T$ exhibit regret scaling with $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$.  This work investigates MAB and SLB, leveraging quantum reward oracles.  We present quantum algorithms for both models achieving regret bounds of $O(\text{poly}(\log T))$, representing an exponential improvement over the classical dependence on $T$.  To the best of our knowledge, this constitutes the first demonstrably quantum-accelerated solution for bandit regret and, more broadly, for exploitation in reinforcement learning.  Crucially, our quantum input model is simpler than previous approaches, requiring only quantum oracles for individual arms.

Employing Lorentz-boosted meson wave functions, consistent with the constituent quark model, we demonstrate a more intricate angular dependence within the annihilation amplitudes.  This enhancement in angular dependence, in turn, leads to a greater contribution from higher partial waves ($J>1$) compared to traditional analyses.  This approach provides insight into the purportedly short annihilation range and its correlation with the angular distribution of final-state mesons.

The results are illustrated specifically for broadband filters commonly employed in imaging distant galaxy star clusters, including those of the Hubble Space Telescope (HST)/Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) and the JWST/Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam). Numerous ellipse detection algorithms have emerged and been extensively studied; however, accurately and efficiently identifying ellipses in real-world imagery continues to pose a significant challenge.  This paper presents an industry-focused ellipse detector, leveraging arc-support line segments, that achieves a superior balance between detection accuracy and computational efficiency.  To simplify the complex curves inherent in images while preserving essential properties such as convexity and orientation, the algorithm initially extracts arc-support line segments.  These segments form the foundation for successful ellipse identification.  Consecutive arc-support segments implicitly associated with a common ellipse are iteratively and robustly linked to generate arc-support groups.  The algorithm then adopts a dual approach: local selection of the most salient arc-support group and global search of all valid paired groups, thereby rapidly fitting initial ellipse approximations.  Subsequently, a hierarchical clustering technique is applied to the five-dimensional parameter space of the initial ellipses, generating a candidate set of ellipses.  Finally, a rigorous and effective verification process selects and refines the most salient ellipse candidates, producing the final detections. Recent LHCb and Belle measurements of $R_K$ and $R_{K^*}$ motivate a systematic investigation, employing effective field theory, of potential New Physics (NP) contributions to $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ transitions.  This investigation focuses on deviations from Lepton Flavour Universality (LFU) within both the Weak Effective Theory (WET) and the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT).

Within the WET, regardless of the methodology used to account for hadronic uncertainties, the data strongly suggests scenarios involving the simultaneous presence of two operators: a left-handed quark current coupled to the muon vector current and a right-handed quark current coupled to the muon axial current.

Conversely, within the SMEFT, the interpretation of the data concerning hadronic effects significantly influences the inferred NP scenarios.  A stringent treatment of hadronic uncertainties favors the simultaneous presence of two operators: one with a left-handed quark and muon coupling and another with a left-handed quark and right-handed muon coupling.  However, a more conservative approach to estimating hadronic matrix elements allows for a wider range of viable scenarios, including those characterized by the presence of only the purely left-handed operator with muon coupling.

This study systematically investigates quantum correlations near a black hole, leveraging the framework of measurement-induced nonlocality (MIN).  We examine the quantum metrics governing fermionic, bosonic, and mixed fermion-boson modes in the context of Hawking radiation, employing a unified analytical approach.  Our findings reveal a critical distinction in the asymptotic limit:  only fermionic correlations persist in the infinite Hawking temperature regime.  Conversely, while higher-frequency modes exhibit sustained correlations at finite Hawking temperatures, mixed systems exhibit a greater sensitivity to increases in fermionic frequencies compared to bosonic frequencies.  The rapid diminishment of MIN for the latter modes suggests that elevated frequencies may constitute a viable mechanism for maintaining nonlocal correlations within finite-temperature scenarios.

A rigorous theoretical foundation for reconstructing the RFI framework from the Fisher information matrix (FIM) framework is thus established. This study investigates the prevalence and characteristics of deceptive online reviews, focusing specifically on restaurant experiences documented on Google. This study's results have broader implications for understanding and mitigating deceptive behavior, including the dissemination of misinformation, and offer a quantifiable measure of potentially antisocial tendencies through the lens of public trust.  The research also outlines future research directions and acknowledges limitations.

This paper presents an exact relaxation framework for minimizing objectives incorporating the total variation of binary-valued functions (of bounded variation), leveraging the co-area formula.  The applicability of this approach spans a broad spectrum of important problems, including binary image restoration, segmentation, minimal compliance topology optimization, and the optimal design of composite membranes, among others.  Critically, the relaxation procedure transforms the binary constraint into a box constraint.  We demonstrate that thresholding a solution to the relaxed problem almost certainly yields a solution to the original binary-valued optimization problem.  The robustness of the solutions under data perturbations is analyzed, and extensions incorporating volume constraints, relevant for structural optimization applications, are explored.  To facilitate efficient numerical computation of the relaxed problem, a locally superlinearly convergent algorithm is developed. This algorithm relies on exact penalization, Fenchel duality, and a semismooth Newton method.  The paper concludes with a presentation of numerical results, focusing on applications within mathematical image processing.

Current anxiety and depression screening methodologies are demonstrably inadequate for effective monitoring and treatment. Contemporary software systems frequently exhibit high configurability, enabling diverse stakeholders to tailor their functionalities.  Precisely understanding the correlation between configuration parameters and desired performance metrics is crucial for enhancing system controllability and optimization, but has historically been a significant knowledge gap due to the inherent opacity of configuration interaction.  Prior performance analysis efforts frequently treat configurations as isolated data points, neglecting the inherent spatial relationships within the configuration space.  This methodological limitation precludes exploration of critical aspects of the configuration landscape, such as local optima.  This work proposes a novel paradigm for performance analysis: modelling the configuration space as a structured "fitness landscape."  To substantiate this approach, we developed a novel, open-source framework, termed Fitness Landscape Analysis (FLA), leveraging graph data mining techniques.  Applying FLA to a comprehensive dataset comprising 86 million benchmarked configurations drawn from 32 workloads across three real-world systems, yielded six key insights.  These findings, collectively, provide a comprehensive characterization of the landscape's topography.  Subsequent detailed discussions explore the implications of these insights for both system configuration tuning and predictive performance modeling.

Equational unification is a crucial problem in automated theorem proving and security protocol analysis.  This paper focuses on XOR-unification, the unification problem modulo the theory of exclusive-or.  This theory is characterized by the exclusive-or operator, which is associative, commutative, nilpotent, and possesses an identity element. The influence of missing data on the acquisition of signal structure through principal component analysis (PCA) warrants investigation.  Prior research (Biehl and Mietzner, 1993) establishes a critical dependence between sample size, dimensionality, and the efficacy of signal structure learning, highlighting a threshold for observation count below which learning does not commence.  This study extends that analysis to incorporate missing data.  Probabilistic PCA, a prevalent method for inferring signal structure in incomplete datasets, is employed.  Our analytical findings suggest that the presence of missing data fundamentally alters the signal-to-noise ratio rather than diminishing the effective sample size, as often assumed.  This theoretical prediction of a phase transition in learning curves is corroborated by simulations and empirical analyses of real-world data.

Diffusion-driven processes represent crucial phenomena within materials science, particularly in the context of energy conversion and transport.  In electrochemical energy conversion, species diffusion is intrinsically linked to the rate of energy exchange and, consequently, the performance of the resultant device.  Conversely, the propagation of electric fields through any medium can induce species diffusion.  This effect, while potentially exploitable for the modulation of surface nanostructures, can also lead to uncontrolled morphological changes, potentially resulting in irreversible degradation of metallic conductors.  Thus, comprehending material behavior in the presence of diffusive driving forces is of significant scientific import.  This dissertation undertakes a focused investigation of specific examples of species diffusion during both energy conversion and transport processes.  Specifically, the study examines lithium intercalation into cathode electrodes of lithium-ion batteries and the morphological evolution of inclusions subjected to electromigration in metallic conductors.  The dissertation demonstrates the efficacy of phase-field methodologies in accurately representing the key physical mechanisms governing these diffusion-driven phenomena.

Statistical model selection necessitates criteria for discerning the optimal model from a candidate set, balancing goodness-of-fit against model complexity. This paper introduces a novel family of robust model selection criteria specifically designed for independent but not identically distributed (i.n.i.d.) observations.  These criteria leverage Rényi's pseudodistance (RP), a metric offering a tunable trade-off between efficiency and robustness.  A critical tuning parameter, α, governs this balance.  The paper derives theoretical properties of the RP-based criterion, providing explicit expressions for the criterion within the framework of multiple linear regression.  Furthermore, the analysis extends to encompass nested model structures, yielding corresponding explicit expressions.  Finally, a simulation study corroborates the empirical robustness advantages of the proposed method.

This paper investigates utility indifference valuation (UIV) of contingent claims under a simplified framework where traded and non-traded assets are uncorrelated, but the claim's pricing may depend on both asset classes. Focusing on European-style claims and leveraging the Gaussian structure of the model, we employ a BSDE technique, specifically a Malliavin-type representation theorem (Ma, 2002), to demonstrate the regularity of the pricing function and characterize the UIP for potentially discontinuous European payoffs as a viscosity solution of a suitable partial differential equation (PDE) with continuous spatial derivatives.

The optimal hedging strategy is shown to be essentially equivalent to a delta-hedging strategy corresponding to the UIP.  Since closed-form solutions are typically unavailable, we derive asymptotic expansions for prices and hedging strategies in the limit of small risk aversion.

Baryon acoustic oscillations (BAOs), imprinted in the large-scale structure by primordial fluctuations, serve as standard rulers for cosmological distance measurements. In contrast, a clear BAO signal emerges from the clustering of overlapping voids, which effectively sample the density field minima.  These overlapping void catalogs were constructed using Delaunay triangulation of galaxy positions, identifying the centers of empty circumspheres enclosed by tetrahedra.

We achieve a statistically significant detection (greater than 3σ) of BAOs in void distributions using the largest publicly available sample of luminous red galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS)-III Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) Data Release 11.  This represents the first observational detection of BAOs in voids.

This loss function encourages the model to predict not just the precise visual token index, but also the correct cluster containing that token.  Even with prediction errors in token selection, the cluster-centric approach significantly increases the likelihood of generating visually coherent and robust outputs.

Robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) have emerged as a powerful framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, driven by advancements in robust optimization and reinforcement learning. This review comprehensively examines the evolution and advancements in RMDP formulations, focusing on ambiguity modeling. We summarize three prevalent rectangular conditions and present a novel proof establishing the NP-hardness of non-rectangular RMDPs.  Furthermore, the review extends beyond traditional RMDP formulations, exploring recent research that relaxes or avoids rectangular assumptions.  These advancements lead to more flexible and pragmatic modeling approaches, thereby enhancing the adaptability and efficacy of RMDPs in real-world applications.

Quantum steering, a quantum correlation intermediate to entanglement and nonlocality, has become a critical resource for various quantum information processing tasks, including quantum key distribution and true randomness generation.  Accurate detection and quantification of quantum steering are paramount for these applications.  While semi-definite programming (SDP) provides a valuable framework for quantifying steerability,  a significant computational hurdle arises from the unknown optimal measurement strategy, leading to protracted computation times for evaluating steerable measures for arbitrary quantum states.  Furthermore, the SDP approach necessitates complete quantum state characterization through tomography, a process often demanding substantial resources and complexity.  This work leverages a semi-supervised self-training model to estimate steerable weights, a key metric of quantum steering.  This model's capacity to learn from limited labeled data drastically reduces the labeling effort.  Feature extraction, crucial for model training, is achieved by utilizing probabilities derived from projective measurements performed on target states subjected to arbitrary local unitary transformations. This approach circumvents the need for quantum state tomography.  Demonstrating robust generalization capabilities, the model achieves high precision with limited resource expenditure.

The Pareto optimal set in smooth, convex multiobjective optimization problems exhibits a diffeomorphic structure akin to an (m-1)-dimensional simplex. This hierarchical arrangement of submanifolds constitutes a stratification, with the union of these manifolds forming a stratified set, encompassing the entirety of the Pareto optimal solutions.  This paper investigates the generalization of these geometric structures to non-convex optimization scenarios.  Existing results are reviewed, and potential implications for the development of specialized optimization algorithms are explored.

This study presents an exact solution to the equations of motion for a two-field cosmological model exhibiting multi-field dark energy.  The model is characterized by field-space trajectories exhibiting consistently high turning rates.  We investigate a specific class of two-field models and demonstrate that these trajectories, which lead to accelerated spacetime expansion, can arise even when the scalar potential preserves the rotational symmetry of the field-space metric.  Focusing on a Poincaré disk field space, we analytically derive the scalar potential form compatible with these background solutions.  Furthermore, we obtain the exact solutions.  These solutions exhibit field-space trajectories spiraling inward towards the center of the Poincaré disk. Notably, the functional form of the derived scalar potential is compatible with a hidden symmetry, although this symmetry is explicitly broken by the inclusion of a constant term.

Real-world multivariate time series, encompassing sensor readings and network data, exhibit anomalous fluctuations attributable to mechanical defects. Addressing the inherent challenges of unsupervised time series anomaly detection, this study introduces a novel self-supervised learning paradigm.  Leveraging a data degradation scheme, we synthesize four distinct outlier types and systematically substitute portions of the input data with these anomalies.  Inspired by the self-attention mechanism, a Transformer-based architecture, termed AnomalyBERT, is developed to efficiently capture temporal context and identify anomalous patterns.  This architecture converts multivariate data points into contextualized temporal representations incorporating relative positional biases.  Subsequently, anomaly scores are derived from these representations.  Empirical evaluation on five diverse real-world benchmark datasets demonstrates AnomalyBERT's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.  The associated source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Jhryu30/AnomalyBERT.
